anchors.text: The bag was not where I had left it. I look everywhere. I go to the class and the playground. I am very sad. Then my friend come and he say he have my bag. I am happy. The end.

The bag was not where I had left it. I had put it under the bench near the bus stop while I bought a samosa, and now it was gone. My books, my lunch and my new calculator were inside. I felt sick. I asked the samosa seller, but he did not see anything. Then I saw a small boy running down the street with a blue bag. I ran after him and shouted. When I caught up, he was crying. He said he thought someone forgot it and he was taking it to the police station. I felt bad for shouting. I thanked him and we walked back together. After that day, I never leave my bag anywhere.

The bag was not where I had left it. For a moment I simply stared at the empty space under the bench, as if staring hard enough might bring it back. Inside were my notebooks, my lunch and, worst of all, the drawings I had spent the whole holiday finishing for the art competition.

I checked behind the bench, then under the next one, then along the platform, my heart thudding louder with every empty corner. Overhead, the announcer's voice echoed, calm and useless.

It was the tea-seller who finally pointed, without a word, towards the lost-property window. Behind the glass, perched on a pile of umbrellas, sat my bag. A cleaner had found it and handed it in only minutes before.

When I unzipped it, the drawings were still there, a little creased at one corner. I smoothed them flat on my knee. That afternoon I won second prize, but what I remember most is the cleaner's shy smile when I went back to thank her.

anchors.text: We should plant trees. Trees are good. Trees are green and nice. I like trees. Please plant more trees in the school. Thank you.

Plant More Trees!

Our school should plant more trees. Firstly, trees give us shade. In summer our playground is very hot and students cannot play there in the afternoon. If we have more trees, it will be cooler. Secondly, trees make the air clean. There is a lot of traffic near our school, so we need clean air. Also, trees are homes for birds and squirrels and it is nice to see them. Some people say trees cost money, but saplings are cheap and students can look after them. So I think we should plant trees this monsoon. Let's do it together!

Green Up Our Grounds

On a May afternoon, our playground is a sheet of hot concrete where nobody wants to play. It does not have to be this way. Planting trees around the grounds would make our school cooler, healthier and more beautiful.

The most urgent reason is heat. A large tree can make the air beneath it noticeably cooler, giving us shaded places to play and eat. Trees would also catch some of the dust from the busy road outside our gates.

Some may argue that trees are expensive and need care. However, saplings cost little, and if each class adopted and watered its own tree, students would learn responsibility along the way.

The monsoon is the perfect time to plant. Let us ask the Principal to support a tree-planting week, so that the students who come after us can enjoy the shade we planted.

anchors.text: In 2015 40% students walk to school and in 2025 25% walk. Bus is 30% and 35%. Car is 10% and 30%. Bicycle is 20% and 10%. Car is more. Walking is less.

The table shows how students at Green Valley School travelled to school in 2015 and 2025. The biggest change is in cars. In 2015 only 10% came by car but in 2025 it was 30%, so it became three times more. Walking went down from 40% to 25% and cycling also went down from 20% to 10%. The bus went up a little, from 30% to 35%. Overall, more students come by car and less students walk or cycle. This may be because families live further away now.

The table compares how students at Green Valley School travelled to school in 2015 and 2025. The most striking change is the rise in car journeys, which tripled from 10% to 30%. In contrast, the proportion of students who walked fell from 40% to 25%, and cycling halved from 20% to 10%. Bus travel, however, remained fairly stable, rising only slightly from 30% to 35%. Overall, the figures suggest a clear shift away from walking and cycling towards travelling by car. Consequently, the school may need to consider the effect on traffic near its gates and on students' fitness.
